content: Postpartum iron deficiency anemia is a condition that arises due to significant blood loss during childbirth or insufficient dietary iron intake or absorption. It is characterized by iron deficiency accompanied by a lower-than-normal blood hemoglobin concentration. However, hemoglobin levels can be influenced by factors other than anemia, so they must be interpreted alongside clinical symptoms. Common symptoms of postpartum anemia include fatigue, shortness of breath, and dizziness. Treatment options for postpartum iron deficiency anemia include oral iron supplementation, intravenous iron administration, erythropoietin therapy (which stimulates red blood cell production), and red blood cell transfusion. The goal of treatment is to alleviate symptoms and restore normal hemoglobin levels. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and potential harms of these treatment modalities. The review included 22 randomized controlled trials involving 2,858 women. Most of these studies were assessed to have a high risk of bias, and many comparisons were based on a small number of studies with limited sample sizes. No primary outcome analysis included data from more than two studies. In 10 studies comparing intravenous iron to oral iron (1,553 women), fatigue was reported in two studies. One study showed significant improvement in fatigue favoring the intravenous iron group, while the other did not report this outcome. Other symptoms of anemia were not consistently reported. Serious adverse events were noted in the intravenous iron group, including one death from cardiomyopathy and one case of arrhythmia. Allergic reactions were reported in three women treated with intravenous iron, but the difference was not statistically significant. Gastrointestinal side effects were less frequent in the intravenous iron group compared to the oral iron group. One study compared red blood cell transfusion to no intervention. Fatigue improved significantly in the transfusion group at three days post-treatment, but no difference was observed between the groups at six weeks. Maternal mortality was not reported in this study. Other comparisons included oral iron (with or without additional food substances) versus placebo, intravenous iron combined with oral iron versus oral iron alone, and erythropoietin (alone or combined with iron) versus placebo or iron. These studies did not consistently evaluate fatigue or other clinical symptoms of anemia. Maternal mortality was rarely reported across all studies. The authors concluded that the available evidence does not provide a clear answer regarding the most effective treatment for postpartum iron deficiency anemia. The quality of evidence was generally low, and clinical outcomes were rarely reported. Laboratory measures, such as hemoglobin levels, may not reliably reflect the clinical benefits of treatment. Intravenous iron appeared to have fewer gastrointestinal side effects compared to oral iron, but it was associated with rare but serious adverse events, such as anaphylaxis and cardiac complications. The clinical significance of the modest improvement in fatigue observed with blood transfusion is uncertain, and this benefit must be weighed against potential risks, including maternal mortality and immunological sensitization, which could affect future pregnancies. For oral iron, it remains unclear whether the benefits in alleviating anemia symptoms outweigh the documented gastrointestinal side effects. There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the efficacy of erythropoietin treatment. The authors emphasized the need for further research focusing on clinical outcomes, such as the presence and severity of anemia symptoms, while balancing these against potential harms, including survival and severe morbidity.
